transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-02
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (BlueRidge Head of Platform), Ethan Cole (Cloud Architect), Lillian Wu (Security), Marcus Nguyen (DevOps)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros please, then we can jump into your networking constraints for the private deployment.
[00:18] Priya Rao: Hi all, Priya here — we run the platform team at BlueRidge, healthcare SaaS. Our ask is we want PHI staying in our VPCs, so private deployment / VPC only.
[00:30] Jordan Lee: Perfect, yeah we expect that. Sofia, wanna lead on the networking bits?
[00:35] Sofia Martinez: Sure. Can you give a quick rundown of your current AWS footprint and any Transit Gateway or Direct Connect links?
[00:45] Ethan Cole: We have three accounts — dev/prod/shared, TGW attached for shared services, Direct Connect into our colo, and peering for a couple of legacy apps. We prefer not to add public endpoints for PHI.
[01:00] Sofia Martinez: Got it. A couple of questions up-front: do you have overlapping CIDRs across accounts, and do you want the Redwood nodes in the same VPC or as a peered VPC/service behind PrivateLink?
[01:15] Marcus Nguyen: We do have some older overlaps: prod uses 10.0.0.0/16, shared is 10.1.0.0/16 — but one of our partners still has a 10.0.0.0/16 range which complicates peering.
[01:28] Lillian Wu: From security, we need customer-managed KMS, HSM-backed keys ideally, and full audit logging for all inference requests that touch PHI.
[01:40] Jordan Lee: Totally reasonable. We support customer-managed KMS for encrypting at rest, and we can integrate with HSM in the Private deployment. We'll include our audit log retention options in the pack.
[01:52] Priya Rao: What are the typical patterns customers use? We heard about both VPC peering and PrivateLink. Pros/cons?
[02:05] Sofia Martinez: Two main patterns: (1) VPC peering or Transit Gateway attach where Redwood runs in your account/VPC — gives you full control and private IPs, but requires non-overlapping CIDRs or routing workarounds. (2) PrivateLink — Redwood exposes an interface endpoint/service; this avoids CIDR overlap issues and centralizes updates, but is slightly more operationally decoupled and you manage interface endpoints and endpoint policies.
[02:35] Ethan Cole: For our setup, Transit Gateway is preferred because we want central routing through shared services. Any gotchas with TGW?
[02:45] Sofia Martinez: You can attach our VPC to your TGW or we can peer into your VPC — with TGW you get high-scale routing and easier cross-account topology. Things to watch: TGW route tables, route propagation, and cross-account attachment limits. Also, if you're using Direct Connect with route filters, we'll need the DX team involved for prefix filters.
[03:06] Marcus Nguyen: How do you handle private DNS for endpoint names? We rely on private DNS so services resolve inside our VPC.
[03:15] Sofia Martinez: For PrivateLink we support private DNS so your services hit the interface endpoints transparently. For a VPC-hosted deployment, we recommend route 53 private hosted zones or internal NLBs exposing the service name. We'll share the DNS guidance doc.
[03:30] Jordan Lee: Also worth noting region constraints: which AWS regions do you want this in? We currently have Private deployment options in US-East-1, US-West-2, and eu-west-1 with additional regions by request.
[03:45] Priya Rao: Primary needs are US-East for lowest latency, but also EU residency for one of our EU customers. Can Redwood place nodes in two regions and replicate keys?
[03:56] Sofia Martinez: Multi-region is supported but KMS cross-region implications matter. We can either use a regional CMK per region and replicate control plane configs, or use an external HSM if you need cross-region key replication. We'll list patterns in the security pack.
[04:15] Lillian Wu: About audit logs — do you capture per-request metadata (prompt, truncated content)? And can logs be pushed to our S3 with encryption and restricted IAM roles?
[04:30] Jordan Lee: Yes, we can ship audit logs to your S3 bucket via cross-account role, encrypt with your CMK, and include request metadata as per agreed retention. We can also redact PII on ingest if required.
[04:47] Ethan Cole: Networking specifics: what's the expected number of ENIs and secondary IPs? Our subnets have IP pressure.
[04:55] Sofia Martinez: Node types vary; each instance will attach ENIs. For large clusters we use ENI-based networking with autoscaling; if IP exhaustion is a concern, we can colocate in a VPC you control using C-sizes. We can also use private NLB w/ target type IP to minimize ENI counts. We'll need your subnet sizes to properly size.
[05:20] Marcus Nguyen: Is there a recommended maximum MTU or any fragmentation concerns with NVMe-backed instances?
[05:27] Sofia Martinez: Standard 1500 MTU is typical; large MTU is supported depending on your CNI, but for inference traffic it's rarely an issue.
[05:36] Jordan Lee: Can we talk about failover? If a region goes down, what's the plan?
[05:42] Sofia Martinez: We support automatic fallback to a compatible model in another region if configured. For Private deployments, you can configure cross-region failover policies, but note data replication and KMS keys need separate planning.
[06:00] Priya Rao: Regarding peering, if we have overlapping CIDR with a partner, what are the practical workarounds?
[06:08] Sofia Martinez: Typical approaches: (1) NAT and proxy routing via a shared-services VPC that does SNAT to non-overlapping addresses, (2) run Redwood behind PrivateLink which avoids peering, or (3) route translation appliances — all add some complexity. PrivateLink is often the cleanest for overlaps.
[06:30] Ethan Cole: If we choose PrivateLink, what about throughput and latency? Our inference is latency-sensitive for realtime triage.
[06:38] Sofia Martinez: PrivateLink adds minimal latency (ms-level), but throughput depends on NLB and interface endpoint ENI scaling; we can size the NLB and use multiple AZs. For strict latency SLOs, colocating in your account/VPC is best.
[06:58] Lillian Wu: From a compliance POV we need RBAC, SSO, and fine-grained auditability. Does Redwood support SAML/SSO for operators?
[07:07] Jordan Lee: Yes, we integrate with SAML/SSO and support RBAC at the token and route level. For Private deployments we support an IAM federated model or can integrate with your IdP for endpoint access controls.
[07:22] Priya Rao: Service endpoints for S3 and ECR in the private VPC — any special considerations?
[07:30] Sofia Martinez: If your VPC uses gateway endpoints for S3, that's fine. For ECR and other APIs we recommend interface endpoints or NAT depending on your preference for egress inspection. We can provide a minimal list of AWS endpoints Redwood needs to reach if a controlled egress model is used.
[07:53] Marcus Nguyen: How are patches and upgrades handled in Private? We want to avoid causing downtime for inference traffic.
[08:01] Sofia Martinez: We do rolling upgrades with canary traffic and automatic fallbacks. For Private deployments you control the rollout window; we can coordinate maintenance windows and provide health checks for canaries.
[08:18] Ethan Cole: Any limits on session length or KV cache persistence across requests? We build stateful chat sessions, need per-user KV caching.
[08:27] Sofia Martinez: The runtime supports KV caching and can persist caches to a managed store. For private deployments, we can route cache to an in-VPC cache (Redis) or use local disk-backed caches depending on latency/cost tradeoffs.
[08:42] Jordan Lee: Let's cover the concrete network checklist items we'll need from you for a pilot.
[08:48] Sofia Martinez: We'll need: list of account IDs, VPC IDs and subnets (AZ mapping), CIDR blocks, preferred region(s), preferred pattern (VPC attach vs PrivateLink), security group restrictions, NAT/egress model, and a contact on the DX/DX team.
[09:10] Priya Rao: We'll assemble that. One question — can Redwood handle private endpoints inside a peered VPC if we use cross-account peering?
[09:20] Sofia Martinez: Yes, but with caveats. Interface endpoints don't cross peering; you'd need to create the interface endpoint in the consumer VPC. For peering a running service, either the service runs in consumer VPC or you use NLB+health checks with DNS entries. That's why TGW or PrivateLink are simpler for cross-account access.
[09:44] Ethan Cole: Is there a recommended way to apply endpoint policies for least privilege? We need to restrict who can call model endpoints per team.
[09:53] Jordan Lee: We support token-level policies and can combine them with endpoint policies on PrivateLink. On the infra side, you can restrict which principals can create/enabled endpoints; we'll include suggested IAM policy snippets.
[10:10] Marcus Nguyen: Cost question: will PrivateLink be more expensive than peering or dedicated VPC?
[10:18] Sofia Martinez: PrivateLink has hourly endpoint charges and data processing fees — typically a small premium relative to peering. Dedicated VPC in your account may have lower egress charges but more ops overhead. We'll include a cost estimate in the follow-up.
[10:35] Priya Rao: For HSM, do you need a specific vendor? We use AWS CloudHSM.
[10:43] Sofia Martinez: AWS CloudHSM is supported — we can integrate for key operations. There are also bring-your-own-HSM flows for on-prem HSM clusters in some Private deployments.
[10:55] Lillian Wu: Can we enforce that no plaintext prompts leave our account unencrypted? We need end-to-end encryption during transit and at-rest.
[11:06] Jordan Lee: In transit we use TLS between services; for extra assurance you can use a VPC-hosted deployment so plaintext never leaves your VPC export boundary except to local nodes we host. For at-rest, we encrypt with your CMK. We'll document exact crypto flow in the security pack.
[11:30] Ethan Cole: Is there any requirement for public IPs on instances?
[11:35] Sofia Martinez: Not required. We can run entirely with private IPs and only use NAT gateways for egress to managed services, or proxy egress via shared services.
[11:47] Marcus Nguyen: If we have strict egress inspection, can the nodes push logs to a local forwarder instead of S3?
[11:54] Sofia Martinez: Yep — either push to your forwarder over a private link or write to S3 via cross-account role; we'll support both.
[12:05] Priya Rao: How long does a typical pilot take to validate performance? We need to hit 100ms 95th percentile for small prompts.
[12:15] Jordan Lee: For a standard pilot, 1–2 weeks is realistic: first day on boarding and networking, then signal tests for latency/throughput. We'll run a small benchmark harness against your TGW or PrivateLink endpoint.
[12:28] Ethan Cole: For the benchmark, what metrics and artifacts do you need from us?
[12:34] Sofia Martinez: We'll need a set of representative prompts, target QPS, payload sizes, and an account to run from (or IP ranges). We'll share our benchmark harness and a script to run from your side.
[12:50] Lillian Wu: On the legal/compliance side: data residency and retention. Can we enforce deletion after X days?
[12:58] Jordan Lee: Yes, retention policies can be configured per-customer and we can support deletion windows. For PHI we recommend short retention and explicit consent flows; we'll include retention defaults and deletion APIs in the security pack.
[13:15] Marcus Nguyen: If we do peering, are there any limits on number of routes in your route tables?
[13:22] Sofia Martinez: We try to keep route table entries minimal; TGW route tables scale better. For a direct VPC attach you'll need to ensure your route table can accept propagated routes; if you have many prefixes we might recommend using TGW and a central route table.
[13:40] Ethan Cole: What about rate limiting and throttles — can we set per-tenant limits inside our private deployment?
[13:48] Jordan Lee: Yes, we support per-route and per-token rate limiting and quotas. For dedicated instances you can map tokens to teams and enforce quotas at the platform level.
[14:00] Priya Rao: Any compliance docs you can share now? SOC 2, HIPAA, architecture diagrams?
[14:06] Jordan Lee: We'll send the SOC 2 report summary and a HIPAA addendum where applicable. Sofia will attach the architecture and network checklist.
[14:16] Sofia Martinez: Also feel free to send a sanitized network diagram so we can mark required changes — helps speed the pilot.
[14:26] Priya Rao: For multi-region failover, how do you test consistency for KV caches?
[14:33] Sofia Martinez: We either replicate caches asynchronously or use a central Redis in your shared services VPC. For strict consistency there's always a tradeoff with latency; we'll help you pick a pattern based on your tolerance.
[14:48] Ethan Cole: Is there a way to do a zero-trust style connection? mTLS between your nodes and ours?
[14:55] Sofia Martinez: We can support mTLS for node-to-node if you require it; that is more advanced and we'd treat it as a custom integration in the pilot.
[15:06] Marcus Nguyen: Any special firewall rules for health checks?
[15:10] Sofia Martinez: Health checks hit the NLB or the service port; we'll provide specific IP ranges and ports. If you're using PrivateLink, it's all internal to your VPC so health checks come from your ENIs.
[15:22] Jordan Lee: Let's capture next steps — Jordan will send pricing & comparison, Sofia will send security pack and network checklist, BlueRidge to send CIDRs and TGW config.
[15:35] Priya Rao: Sounds good. One last thing — do you lock model versions for reproducibility? We need deterministic outputs for audit.
[15:44] Jordan Lee: Yes, you can pin model versions and we maintain version hashes; we also support evals and regression alerts on prompts to detect drift.
[16:00] Ethan Cole: Ok we'll aim to get the artifacts by next week. Thanks all.

End of meeting.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional overlaps and filler words removed for readability, some proper nouns guessed (e.g., specific VPC names).
